learn.hook: Draw the graph of a train's distance from Delhi without lifting your pen: no train teleports, so distance is a continuous function of time.
points: Intuitively, f is continuous at x = c if its graph has no break, jump or hole there.
Formally: f is continuous at c if f(c) is defined and lim(x→c) f(x) = f(c), i.e. LHL = RHL = f(c).
If this fails, c is a point of discontinuity (only points in the domain are tested).
f is continuous on an interval if it is continuous at every point of it; a continuous function is continuous at every point of its domain.
The greatest integer function [x] is discontinuous at every integer: just left of 2 it is 1, at 2 it is 2.

example.q: Is f(x) = x + 2 for x ≤ 1 and x − 2 for x > 1 continuous at x = 1?
steps: LHL ≠ RHL, so the limit does not exist.
example.answer: Not continuous at x = 1 (it has a jump).

learn.reallife: Mobile data billing in slabs (₹ per GB jumping at 2 GB, 5 GB) is a step function like [x]: the bill jumps, so it is discontinuous at each slab boundary.

games.title: Test continuity at x = c
items: Find the left-hand limit at c
Find the right-hand limit at c

games.title: Continuity check
items: If LHL = RHL at c, f must be continuous at c.
f(c) must also equal that common limit.
A function can be continuous at a point outside its domain.
Continuity is checked only at points of the domain.
It is continuous at every point of its domain; 0 is not in the domain.

quiz.q: For f(x) = x + 2 (x ≤ 1) and x − 2 (x > 1), what is the right-hand limit at x = 1?
quiz.explain: For x slightly more than 1, f(x) = x − 2 → 1 − 2 = −1.
quiz.mistake: Uses the left piece for the right-hand limit

quiz.q: At which points is f(x) = [x] discontinuous?
quiz.explain: At each integer n, LHL = n − 1 but f(n) = n. Between integers [x] is constant and so continuous.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a step function is continuous because it is defined everywhere

quiz.q: f(x) = 3x − 5 for x ≤ 2 and x² − 3 for x > 2. What is the value of LHL − RHL at x = 2?
quiz.explain: LHL = 6 − 5 = 1 and RHL = 4 − 3 = 1, so LHL − RHL = 0. Also f(2) = 1, so f is continuous at 2.
quiz.mistake: Assumes a piecewise function must jump at the junction

quiz.q: f(x) = 1 for x ≥ 0 and −1 for x < 0. At x = 0, f is
quiz.explain: The two one-sided limits differ, so the limit at 0 does not exist.
quiz.mistake: Checks only f(0) and the right side

quiz.q: Which function is continuous on R?
quiz.explain: |x| has no break anywhere. [x] jumps at integers; the other two jump or blow up at a point.
quiz.mistake: Defines a value at the bad point and thinks that removes the break

quiz.q: f(x) = (x² − 9)/(x − 3) for x ≠ 3 and f(3) = 6. What is lim(x→3) f(x)?
quiz.explain: (x² − 9)/(x − 3) = x + 3 for x ≠ 3, which tends to 6. Since f(3) = 6 too, f is continuous at 3.
quiz.mistake: Substitutes x = 3 directly and gives up on 0/0

quiz.q: If lim(x→c⁻) f(x) = lim(x→c⁺) f(x) = 5 but f(c) = 4, then at c, f is
quiz.explain: The limit exists but does not equal f(c), so the definition of continuity fails.
quiz.mistake: Thinks equal one-sided limits are enough

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The greatest integer function is discontinuous at x = 2.
Reason (R): lim(x→2⁻) [x] = 1 while [2] = 2.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Just left of 2, [x] = 1, but [2] = 2. The mismatch is exactly why [x] is discontinuous at 2.
quiz.mistake: Thinks [x] = 2 just left of 2

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I prove a function is continuous at a point, not just by looking at the graph?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Left limit, right limit and the function value must all match. No jumps, no holes!
teach.nudge: You compared the limits. What else must they be equal to?

learn.hook: Boards love a 3-mark question: 'Find k so that f is continuous.' It is just two limits set equal, and here you master it.
points: Constant, identity, polynomial, modulus, sin x and cos x are continuous everywhere; rational functions and tan x are continuous on their domains.
If f and g are continuous at c, so are f + g, f − g, fg and f/g (when g(c) ≠ 0).
A composition of continuous functions is continuous: |sin x|, sin(x²), cos|x|, e^(sin x).
For a piecewise function, the only doubtful points are the junctions; check LHL = RHL = f(c) there.
To find unknown constants, equate the left and right values at each junction and solve.

example.q: Find k so that f(x) = kx + 1 (x ≤ 5) and 3x − 5 (x > 5) is continuous at x = 5.

learn.reallife: Highway engineers join a straight road to a curved ramp. The two formulas must give the same height at the joint, the same 'equate both sides' step that finds k.

quiz.q: Find k if f(x) = kx² (x ≤ 2) and 3 (x > 2) is continuous at x = 2.
quiz.explain: LHL = f(2) = 4k and RHL = 3, so 4k = 3 and k = 3/4.
quiz.mistake: Uses 2k instead of 4k (forgets to square 2)

quiz.q: f(x) = ax + 1 (x ≤ 3) and bx + 3 (x > 3) is continuous at x = 3. What is a − b?
quiz.mistake: Makes a sign slip moving constants across

quiz.q: For f(x) = λ(x² − 2x) when x ≤ 0 and 4x + 1 when x > 0, which is true?
options: f is continuous at 0 when λ = 1
f is continuous at 0 when λ = 0
f is continuous at 0 for every λ
f is discontinuous at x = 0 for every λ
quiz.explain: LHL = f(0) = λ(0) = 0 while RHL = 1. No λ can make 0 equal 1.
quiz.mistake: Tries to solve for λ without noticing it multiplies zero

quiz.q: Find k if f(x) = (sin x)/x for x ≠ 0 and f(0) = k is continuous at 0.
quiz.explain: lim(x→0) (sin x)/x = 1, so continuity needs k = 1.
quiz.mistake: Substitutes x = 0 and takes the limit as 0

quiz.q: Why is f(x) = |sin x| continuous everywhere?
options: It is the composition of the continuous functions sin x and |x|
quiz.explain: A composition of continuous functions is continuous. (It is not differentiable at multiples of π, so the last reason is false.)
quiz.mistake: Thinks boundedness or periodicity gives continuity

quiz.q: f(x) = x + 1 for x ≥ 1 and x² + 1 for x < 1. How many points of discontinuity does f have?
quiz.explain: Each piece is a polynomial. At x = 1: LHL = 2, RHL = 2, f(1) = 2. So f is continuous everywhere.
quiz.mistake: Assumes every junction is a point of discontinuity

quiz.q: If f and g are continuous at x = 2 with g(2) = 0, which might fail to be continuous at x = 2?
quiz.explain: Sums, differences and products of continuous functions are continuous. f/g needs g(2) ≠ 0.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the condition on the denominator

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): f(x) = sin(x²) is continuous on R.
Reason (R): The sum of two continuous functions is continuous.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
quiz.explain: A is true because sin(x²) is a composition of continuous functions. R is true but is about sums, not composition.
quiz.mistake: Uses a correct rule that does not apply here

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I find the k that makes a piecewise function continuous?'
teach.praise: Chirp! At the joining point, make the left value equal the right value and solve for k. Smooth sailing!
teach.nudge: Where exactly do you check, and what do you set equal there?

learn.hook: A V-shaped graph has no break but has a sharp corner. Continuous, yes. Differentiable, no. That one corner hides a whole idea.
points: f is differentiable at c if the left and right derivatives lim(h→0) [f(c + h) − f(c)]/h are equal and finite.
Differentiable ⇒ continuous, but continuous does not imply differentiable: |x| is continuous at 0 but has no derivative there.
Standard rules from Class XI: (u ± v)′ = u′ ± v′, (uv)′ = u′v + uv′, (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v².
Chain rule: if y = f(g(x)), then dy/dx = f′(g(x)) · g′(x). Differentiate the outside, keep the inside, multiply by the inside's derivative.
[x] is not differentiable at integers (not even continuous); |x − 1| is not differentiable at x = 1.

steps: Outer function: sin u, with u = x².
d/du (sin u) = cos u, and du/dx = 2x.

learn.reallife: Mission control tracks a rocket's height h(t) and its vertical speed v(t) = h′(t). Speed is a derivative, and the chain rule converts rates when altitude depends on time through another variable.

games.title: Differentiable or not?
items: Left derivative is −1, right derivative is 1.
Differentiability at c implies continuity at c.
|x| is continuous at 0 but not differentiable.
It has a corner at x = 1.
It is not even continuous at 1.

quiz.q: What is d/dx [cos(x³)]?
quiz.explain: Chain rule: −sin(x³) × 3x².
quiz.mistake: Forgets to multiply by the derivative of the inside

quiz.q: If y = (3x − 2)⁴, what is dy/dx at x = 1?
quiz.mistake: Drops the factor 3 from the inside

quiz.q: What is d/dx [sec(tan √x)]?
quiz.explain: Three layers: sec → tan → √x. Multiply sec u tan u, then sec²(√x), then 1/(2√x).
quiz.mistake: Stops after one or two layers of the chain

quiz.q: For f(x) = |x| at x = 0, what are the left and right derivatives?
quiz.explain: Left: (|h| − 0)/h = −h/h = −1 for h < 0. Right: h/h = 1 for h > 0. They differ, so |x| is not differentiable at 0.
quiz.mistake: Swaps the one-sided derivatives

quiz.q: At which point is f(x) = |x − 1| + |x − 3| NOT differentiable?
quiz.explain: Each modulus has a corner where its inside is zero: at x = 1 and x = 3.
quiz.mistake: Looks for the midpoint instead of the zeros of each modulus

quiz.q: If f(x) = sin(2x), what is f′(π/6)?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the factor 2 from the chain rule

quiz.q: Which statement is correct?
options: If f is continuous at c, then f is differentiable at c
A function with a corner at c is not continuous at c
If f is differentiable at c, then f is continuous at c
Polynomials are differentiable only at integers
quiz.explain: Differentiability is the stronger condition: it forces continuity, not the other way round.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the direction of the implication

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): f(x) = |x| is continuous at x = 0 but not differentiable there.
Reason (R): The left-hand derivative and the right-hand derivative of |x| at 0 are unequal.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.explain: LHD = −1 ≠ RHD = 1, so the derivative does not exist at 0, while LHL = RHL = f(0) = 0 gives continuity. R explains the non-differentiability in A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks continuity and differentiability always go together

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: '|x| has no break at 0. So why can't I differentiate it there? And how does the chain rule work?'
teach.praise: Tweet! A corner gives unequal one-sided slopes, so no derivative. And chain rule: derivative of outside times derivative of inside!
teach.nudge: What happens to the slopes on the left and right of 0 for |x|?

topics.title: Implicit functions and inverse trig derivatives

learn.hook: x² + xy + y² = 100 is an oval, not a formula for y. You can still find its slope at any point, without ever solving for y.
points: Implicit differentiation: differentiate both sides with respect to x, treating y as a function of x, so d/dx(y²) = 2y dy/dx and d/dx(xy) = y + x dy/dx. Then solve for dy/dx.
d/dx (sin⁻¹ x) = 1/√(1 − x²) and d/dx (cos⁻¹ x) = −1/√(1 − x²), for −1 < x < 1.
d/dx (tan⁻¹ x) = 1/(1 + x²) for all real x.
Simplify before differentiating: with x = tan θ, sin⁻¹(2x/(1 + x²)) = 2 tan⁻¹ x for |x| < 1, so its derivative is 2/(1 + x²).
Similarly, tan⁻¹[(3x − x³)/(1 − 3x²)] = 3 tan⁻¹ x for |x| < 1/√3.

example.q: Find dy/dx if x² + xy + y² = 100.

learn.reallife: Car and product designers describe smooth body curves by equations in x and y; implicit differentiation gives the slope of such a curve at any point without solving for y.

games.title: Implicit differentiation of xy + y² = tan x + y
items: Differentiate each term with respect to x
y + x y′ + 2y y′ = sec²x + y′
Collect y′ terms: y′(x + 2y − 1) = sec²x − y

quiz.q: If 2x + 3y = sin x, what is dy/dx?
quiz.explain: 2 + 3 dy/dx = cos x ⇒ dy/dx = (cos x − 2)/3.
quiz.mistake: Moves 2 across without changing its sign

quiz.q: If x² + y² = 25, what is dy/dx at the point (3, 4)?
quiz.mistake: Inverts the ratio and writes −y/x

quiz.q: If xy = 12, what is dy/dx at (3, 4)?
quiz.mistake: Uses −x/y as for a circle

quiz.q: What is the derivative of cos⁻¹ x at x = 0?
quiz.explain: d/dx cos⁻¹ x = −1/√(1 − x²), which is −1 at x = 0.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the negative sign

quiz.q: If y = sin⁻¹(2x/(1 + x²)) with |x| < 1, then dy/dx equals
quiz.explain: Put x = tan θ: 2x/(1 + x²) = sin 2θ, so y = 2θ = 2 tan⁻¹ x and y′ = 2/(1 + x²).
quiz.mistake: Differentiates without simplifying and makes an algebra slip

quiz.q: If y = tan⁻¹[(3x − x³)/(1 − 3x²)] for −1/√3 < x < 1/√3, then dy/dx equals
quiz.explain: With x = tan θ, the expression is tan 3θ, so y = 3θ = 3 tan⁻¹ x and y′ = 3/(1 + x²).
quiz.mistake: Misses that the bracket is tan 3θ

quiz.q: If y = sin⁻¹(2x√(1 − x²)) for −1/√2 < x < 1/√2, then dy/dx equals
quiz.explain: Put x = sin θ: 2 sin θ cos θ = sin 2θ, so y = 2θ = 2 sin⁻¹ x and y′ = 2/√(1 − x²).
quiz.mistake: Forgets the factor 2 from the double angle

quiz.q: What is d/dx [tan⁻¹(2x)] at x = 1?
quiz.explain: d/dx tan⁻¹(2x) = 2/(1 + 4x²); at x = 1 this is 2/5.
quiz.mistake: Uses 1 + 2x² or forgets the chain factor 2

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I find dy/dx when y is tangled up with x and I can't solve for y?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Differentiate every term, use the chain rule on y-terms, then collect dy/dx and solve. No untangling needed!
teach.nudge: What extra factor appears when you differentiate y² with respect to x?

learn.hook: Your SIP grows exponentially and the Richter scale uses logarithms. Calculus treats both with two beautifully simple rules.
points: Exponential function bˣ (b > 0, b ≠ 1): domain R, range (0, ∞), passes through (0, 1). The most important base is e ≈ 2.718.
logₐ x is the inverse of aˣ: logₐ x = y ⇔ aʸ = x, defined for x > 0. log x (natural log) means base e in this chapter.
Laws: log(pq) = log p + log q, log(p/q) = log p − log q, log(pⁿ) = n log p, change of base: logₐ p = log p / log a.
d/dx (eˣ) = eˣ and d/dx (log x) = 1/x for x > 0.
With the chain rule: d/dx e^(f(x)) = f′(x) e^(f(x)) and d/dx log f(x) = f′(x)/f(x).

steps: Outer: log u with u = cos eˣ, so dy/du = 1/cos eˣ.

learn.reallife: The pH scale used in chemistry labs is −log₁₀[H⁺]: each step down in pH means ten times more hydrogen ions, a logarithm at work.

quiz.q: What is d/dx [e^(2x)] at x = 0?
quiz.explain: d/dx e^(2x) = 2e^(2x); at x = 0 this is 2e⁰ = 2.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the chain factor 2

quiz.q: What is d/dx [log(x² + 1)] at x = 1?
quiz.explain: Derivative is 2x/(x² + 1); at x = 1 this is 2/2 = 1.
quiz.mistake: Writes 1/(x² + 1) without the chain factor 2x

quiz.q: Which is equal to log 12 (natural log)?
quiz.explain: 12 = 2² × 3, so log 12 = log 4 + log 3 = 2 log 2 + log 3.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the log of a product is the product of logs

quiz.q: What is the domain of log x?
quiz.explain: The logarithm is defined only for positive inputs; log 0 is undefined.
quiz.mistake: Includes 0 in the domain

quiz.q: What is d/dx [e^(sin x)]?
quiz.explain: Chain rule: e^(sin x) times the derivative of sin x.
quiz.mistake: Treats e^(f(x)) like a power and brings the exponent down

quiz.q: If y = log(log x) for x > 1, then dy/dx equals
quiz.explain: dy/dx = (1/log x) × (1/x).
quiz.mistake: Stops after the outer derivative

quiz.q: Using change of base, log₈ 2 equals
quiz.explain: log₈ 2 = log 2 / log 8 = log 2 / (3 log 2) = 1/3.
quiz.mistake: Inverts the ratio and gets 3

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The graph of y = eˣ passes through (0, 1).
Reason (R): The derivative of eˣ is eˣ.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true because e⁰ = 1. R is also true, but it is about slopes, not about the point (0, 1).
quiz.mistake: Links two true facts that are unrelated

teach.ask: Gappu squeaks: 'What are the derivatives of eˣ and log x, and how do I use them with the chain rule?'
teach.praise: Tweet! eˣ stays eˣ, log x gives 1/x, and the chain rule multiplies by the inside's derivative. Super simple!
teach.nudge: What do you multiply by when the exponent or the log's input is not just x?

learn.hook: How do you differentiate xˣ? The power rule fails and the exponential rule fails. Take a log first, and the problem melts.
points: For y = u(x)^v(x), take logs: log y = v log u. Differentiate implicitly: (1/y) dy/dx = v′ log u + v u′/u.
So dy/dx = u^v [v′ log u + v u′/u]. Example: d/dx (xˣ) = xˣ(1 + log x).
Long products and quotients: log y = sum of logs turns products into sums, which are easy to differentiate.
aˣ = e^(x log a), so d/dx (aˣ) = aˣ log a.
Equations like xʸ = yˣ: take logs (y log x = x log y), then differentiate implicitly.

steps: log y = sin x · log x.
(1/y) dy/dx = cos x · log x + sin x · (1/x).
example.answer: dy/dx = x^(sin x) [cos x log x + (sin x)/x]

learn.reallife: Economists measure growth rates and elasticities with logarithms, since d(log y) = dy/y is the relative (percentage) change in y.

games.title: Differentiate y = xˣ
items: Take log: log y = x log x
Multiply by y: dy/dx = xˣ(1 + log x)

quiz.q: If y = xˣ, what is dy/dx at x = 1?
quiz.explain: dy/dx = xˣ(1 + log x); at x = 1, this is 1 × (1 + 0) = 1.
quiz.mistake: Uses the power rule x · x^(x − 1)

quiz.q: What is d/dx (3ˣ)?
quiz.explain: 3ˣ = e^(x log 3), so the derivative is 3ˣ log 3.
quiz.mistake: Applies the power rule to an exponential

quiz.q: If xʸ = yˣ, then dy/dx equals
options: y(x log y − y) / [x(y log x − x)]
quiz.explain: y log x = x log y ⇒ y′ log x + y/x = log y + (x/y) y′ ⇒ y′(log x − x/y) = log y − y/x. Multiply top and bottom by xy.
quiz.mistake: Takes logs but forgets the product rule on y log x

quiz.q: If y = (log x)^(cos x), which expression is dy/dx?
options: (log x)^(cos x) [sin x log(log x) + cos x/(x log x)]
(log x)^(cos x) [cos x/(x log x) − sin x log(log x)]
quiz.explain: log y = cos x · log(log x). Differentiating: −sin x log(log x) + cos x · 1/(x log x). Multiply by y.
quiz.mistake: Gets the sign of the derivative of cos x wrong

quiz.q: Why do we take logarithms before differentiating xˣ?
options: Because log x is easy to integrate
Because the power rule always fails
Because both the base and the exponent depend on x
quiz.explain: Neither the power rule (constant exponent) nor the exponential rule (constant base) applies, but logs turn the power into a product.
quiz.mistake: Thinks logs are needed whenever an exponent appears

quiz.q: If y = (x − 1)(x − 2)/[(x − 3)(x − 4)], then (1/y) dy/dx equals
quiz.explain: log y = log(x − 1) + log(x − 2) − log(x − 3) − log(x − 4) (on a suitable interval). Differentiate term by term.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the denominator factors give negative terms

quiz.q: If y = 2ˣ, what is dy/dx at x = 0?
quiz.explain: dy/dx = 2ˣ log 2; at x = 0, 2⁰ = 1, so the value is log 2.
quiz.mistake: Treats 2ˣ like eˣ

quiz.q: For y = x^(sin x), what is the value of (1/y)(dy/dx) at x = π/2?
quiz.explain: (1/y) dy/dx = cos x log x + sin x/x. At π/2: 0 · log(π/2) + 1/(π/2) = 2/π.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the sin x/x term

quiz.q: Differentiate y = (x² + 1)(x + 3) by taking logs, and check your answer with the product rule. What is dy/dx at x = 1?
quiz.explain: log y = log(x² + 1) + log(x + 3), so dy/dx = y[2x/(x² + 1) + 1/(x + 3)] = 2x(x + 3) + (x² + 1) = 3x² + 6x + 1. The product rule gives the same expression. At x = 1: 3 + 6 + 1 = 10.
quiz.mistake: Keeps only one of the two terms (2x(x + 3) = 8 or x² + 1 = 2) after differentiating

teach.ask: Gappu is stumped: 'How on earth do I differentiate x to the power x?'
teach.praise: Chirp-chirp! Log both sides, differentiate with the product rule, then multiply by y. xˣ tamed!
teach.nudge: What do you do first, before differentiating at all?

learn.hook: A point on a bicycle tyre traces a cycloid. Its x and y each depend on the angle turned. To find the slope, let the angle do the work.
points: A curve can be given by x = f(t), y = g(t), where t is a parameter.
dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt), provided dx/dt ≠ 0.
Parabola x = at², y = 2at: dy/dx = 2a/(2at) = 1/t.
Ellipse x = a cos θ, y = b sin θ: dy/dx = (b cos θ)/(−a sin θ) = −(b/a) cot θ.
Astroid x = a cos³θ, y = a sin³θ: dy/dx = −tan θ. Cycloid x = a(θ − sin θ), y = a(1 + cos θ): dy/dx = −cot(θ/2).

example.q: Find dy/dx if x = a cos³θ and y = a sin³θ.
steps: dy/dx = (3a sin²θ cos θ)/(−3a cos²θ sin θ) = −sin θ/cos θ.

learn.reallife: A cricket ball's flight is tracked by Hawk-Eye as x(t) and y(t). Its direction at any instant is dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt).

games.title: Curve ↔ dy/dx
pairs: x = a cos θ, y = b sin θ
x = a cos³θ, y = a sin³θ
x = a(θ − sin θ), y = a(1 + cos θ)

games.title: Parametric facts
items: For x = t, y = t², dy/dx = 2t.
For x = cos θ, y = sin θ, dy/dx = cot θ.
A circle can be written parametrically as x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ.

quiz.q: If x = at² and y = 2at, what is dy/dx?
quiz.explain: dy/dt = 2a and dx/dt = 2at, so dy/dx = 2a/(2at) = 1/t.
quiz.mistake: Divides dx/dt by dy/dt

quiz.q: If x = 4t and y = 4/t, what is dy/dx at t = 2?
quiz.explain: dy/dt = −4/t² and dx/dt = 4, so dy/dx = −1/t² = −1/4 at t = 2.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the negative sign from differentiating 1/t

quiz.q: If x = 2 cos θ and y = 3 sin θ, what is dy/dx?
quiz.explain: dy/dθ = 3 cos θ and dx/dθ = −2 sin θ, so dy/dx = −(3/2) cot θ.
quiz.mistake: Loses the minus sign from d(cos θ)

quiz.q: If x = a(θ − sin θ) and y = a(1 + cos θ), then dy/dx equals
quiz.explain: dy/dθ = −a sin θ and dx/dθ = a(1 − cos θ). −sin θ/(1 − cos θ) = −2 sin(θ/2)cos(θ/2)/(2 sin²(θ/2)) = −cot(θ/2).
quiz.mistake: Uses 1 + cos θ in the denominator or drops the sign

quiz.q: If x = t², y = t³, what is dy/dx at t = 2?
quiz.explain: dy/dt = 3t² and dx/dt = 2t, so dy/dx = 3t/2 = 3 at t = 2.
quiz.mistake: Divides 2t by 3t²

quiz.q: If x = sin t and y = cos 2t, then dy/dx equals
quiz.explain: dy/dt = −2 sin 2t = −4 sin t cos t and dx/dt = cos t, so dy/dx = −4 sin t.
quiz.mistake: Leaves dy/dt undivided

quiz.q: If x = a cos³θ and y = a sin³θ, what is dy/dx at θ = π/4?
quiz.explain: dy/dx = −tan θ = −tan(π/4) = −1.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the minus sign

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): For x = 3t, y = 6t², dy/dx = 4t.
Reason (R): dy/dx = (dy/dt) ÷ (dx/dt).
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: dy/dt = 12t and dx/dt = 3, so dy/dx = 12t/3 = 4t, found using R.
quiz.mistake: Thinks parametric derivatives need eliminating t first

teach.ask: Gappu flaps: 'x and y both depend on t. How do I find dy/dx?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Find dy/dt and dx/dt, then divide: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt). The parameter does the work!
teach.nudge: Which rate goes on top, and which on the bottom?

learn.hook: Velocity is the first derivative of position; acceleration is the second. Second derivatives tell you how fast the change itself is changing.
points: The second derivative d²y/dx² = d/dx(dy/dx), also written y″, y₂ or f″(x).
Explicit functions: just differentiate twice. y = sin x gives y″ = −sin x.
Implicit: differentiate the expression for y′ again, then substitute y′.
Parametric: d²y/dx² = [d/dt(dy/dx)] ÷ (dx/dt), not (d²y/dt²)/(d²x/dt²).
Typical proofs: y = A cos x + B sin x ⇒ y″ + y = 0; y = sin⁻¹ x ⇒ (1 − x²)y″ − xy′ = 0. (Rolle's theorem and the Mean Value Theorem are not in the current syllabus.)

example.q: If y = sin⁻¹ x, show that (1 − x²) y″ − x y′ = 0.
steps: Multiply by √(1 − x²): (1 − x²) y″ − x y′ = 0.

learn.reallife: At the Buddh circuit, a racing car's speedometer shows the first derivative of distance, while the g-force sensor measures the second derivative, acceleration.

y = log x: y″ at x = 1

games.title: Prove y″ + y = 0 for y = 5 cos x − 3 sin x

quiz.q: If y = x³ + tan x, what is y″?
quiz.explain: y′ = 3x² + sec²x. Differentiating sec²x gives 2 sec x · sec x tan x = 2 sec²x tan x.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the chain rule on sec²x

quiz.q: If y = 5 cos x − 3 sin x, then y″ + y equals
quiz.explain: y″ = −5 cos x + 3 sin x = −y, so y″ + y = 0.
quiz.mistake: Makes a sign slip differentiating cos or sin twice

quiz.q: If y = e^(3x), what is y″ at x = 0?
quiz.explain: y′ = 3e^(3x), y″ = 9e^(3x); at x = 0 this is 9.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by 3 only once

quiz.q: If y = log x, what is y″?
quiz.explain: y′ = 1/x = x⁻¹, so y″ = −x⁻² = −1/x².
quiz.mistake: Stops at the first derivative

quiz.q: If x = at² and y = 2at, what is d²y/dx²?
quiz.explain: dy/dx = 1/t. d/dt(1/t) = −1/t². Divide by dx/dt = 2at: −1/(2at³).
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide by dx/dt and stops at −1/t²

quiz.q: If y = A e^(2x) + B e^(−x), which equation does y satisfy?
quiz.mistake: Gets the sign of the y′ term wrong

quiz.q: If y = 3 cos(log x) + 4 sin(log x), which relation holds?
quiz.explain: y′ = [−3 sin(log x) + 4 cos(log x)]/x, so xy′ = −3 sin(log x) + 4 cos(log x). Differentiating: xy″ + y′ = −y/x, i.e. x²y″ + xy′ + y = 0.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the product rule when differentiating xy′

quiz.q: For x² + y² = 1, the expression for y″ is
quiz.explain: y′ = −x/y. y″ = −(y − x y′)/y² = −(y + x²/y)/y² = −(x² + y²)/y³ = −1/y³.
quiz.mistake: Stops at the first derivative or misses the quotient rule

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What is a second derivative, and how do I find it for parametric curves?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Differentiate again; for parametric curves, differentiate dy/dx with respect to t and divide by dx/dt!
teach.nudge: For parametric curves, can you just take d²y/dt² over d²x/dt²?
